scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Lezim originated in the rural villages of Maharashtra and Gujarat as a form of physical conditioning and martial practice.
Historically, it involved heavier implements like the Reedh (a 2.5-foot bamboo pole with iron chains) or the Koyande (a weighted wooden pole), which were used for strength training.
Over time, these evolved into the lighter musical instruments used today.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Lezim is performed during the Ganesh festival (Ganeshotsav) and village Jatras.
It serves as a communal celebration and a display of physical fitness.
In educational and military contexts, it is used as a discipline-building exercise and a rhythmic drill.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is performed by a minimum of 20 dancers, usually in two rows, four rows, or concentric circles.
Dancers follow a sequence of steps that change every few beats, often totaling 25 different movements in a short performance.
The 'ring leader' uses a whistle to announce changes in the choreography.
Watch for Nartakasamuhanni, Samuhanrtyanta nartakam.

Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Linear rows or concentric circles; dancers often interact with partners in opposite rows

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The central instrument is the Lezim, a wooden pole (todanna bandhaleli) with a chain (adakavalelya) and metal discs.
Percussion is provided by the dholki (a narrow drum) and the halagi.
Listen for the Lezim (wooden idiophone), Dholki (drum), Halagi (carmavadya), Cymbals (talasarakhe).
The pulse is 4/4 or 2/4 at about 140 beats a minute.
A dense, percussive soundscape dominated by the deep, resonant thuds of the dholki drum and the sharp, shimmering metallic clatter of dozens of Lezim instruments striking in unison.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Dancers wear vibrant, colorful costumes typical of Maharashtrian folk traditions.
The dance is performed outdoors in various settings, including school grounds for fitness drills, village streets during Jatras (religious processions), and public squares during the Ganesh festival.

scenes.title: The people
narration: While individual dancers are rarely named in folk traditions, the 400 Maharashtrian players who performed at the 1982 Asian Games in Delhi are cited as a significant collective that brought the dance to international attention.
Three main types exist: military lezim (martial art focus, popular in Baroda), talathekya, and samanyajananna.

Lezim is classified as an Indian folk dance and a 'game and martial dance.' It shares formation characteristics with the Garba of Gujarat, particularly in its concentric circle variants (samuhanrtyanta nartakam).

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Lezim is variant of Garbha: Shares the concentric circle formation (samuhanrtyanta nartakam).
Lezim is same region of Phugadi: Another folk dance from Maharashtra often performed in similar festive contexts.

scenes.title: Step A — slowly

scenes.title: Step B — the next layer

scenes.title: Put it together
